title: Ancient & Classical Empires
description: Rome, Persia, Han, Mauryan — patterns of imperial integration

concepts.title: What an Empire Is
concepts.contentHtml:
An empire is a political unit that exercises sovereignty over peoples it considers culturally or politically distinct, typically through some combination of military domination, indirect administration through local elites, and the imposition of a metropolitan elite's institutions on subordinated populations. The historian Charles Maier defines empires by the asymmetric relationship between a metropole and its peripheries; Michael Doyle emphasises that empire involves effective political control of one society by another; Frederick Cooper highlights that empires explicitly preserve cultural and political distinctions between rulers and ruled rather than dissolving them into common citizenship.

Empires are old. The earliest recognisable cases — the Akkadian Empire under Sargon (c. 2334 BCE), the Egyptian New Kingdom, the Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian empires, the Achaemenid Persian Empire — appeared within a few centuries of the first cities. The pattern of a successful state expanding to incorporate populations and territories beyond its core, then governing those subjects through varying mixes of force, bureaucracy, religion, and infrastructure, is one of the most recurrent forms of political organisation in human history.

The Achaemenid Persian Empire (550–330 BCE) under Cyrus, Darius, and their successors covered most of the eastern Mediterranean and Near East — perhaps 50 million subjects at its height. Its administrative innovations — the satrapy system of regional governors, the Royal Road network, standardised coinage, multilingual administration tolerant of local cults — established patterns that subsequent empires (Parthian, Sasanian, Ottoman) drew on for two millennia. The Achaemenid model of tolerant administration through local elites, secured by overwhelming military capability and a relatively light cultural footprint, has been one of the durable templates for imperial governance.

concepts.title: Rome and Its Mediterranean World
concepts.contentHtml:
The Roman Empire is the canonical Western case. Rome's transformation from a small Italian city-state into the dominant Mediterranean power (3rd century BCE through 1st century CE) and from republic to empire (the principate of Augustus, 27 BCE) established institutions that shaped European political imagination for over a millennium.

Rome's distinctive contributions to imperial governance were extensive. Roman law — codified, adaptable, applied to citizens and (with modifications) to subject peoples — provided one of history's most influential legal systems; the Digest compiled by Justinian in the 6th century became the basis for civil-law systems across continental Europe. The extension of citizenship, culminating in Caracalla's 212 CE Constitutio Antoniniana that granted Roman citizenship to all free inhabitants of the empire, was a uniquely successful integration mechanism. Roman infrastructure — roads, aqueducts, harbours, urban grids — bound the empire physically; Roman religious tolerance (with periodic exceptions for Christians and Jews when they refused emperor cult) reduced the costs of cultural integration.

The empire's decline in the West (formally ending with the deposition of Romulus Augustulus in 476 CE) and continuation in the East as the Byzantine Empire (until 1453) raise the recurring question of why empires fall. The historiography is enormous and contested: Edward Gibbon's Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (1776–1789) emphasised civic virtue and Christianity; modern accounts by Peter Heather, Bryan Ward-Perkins, and others emphasise external pressures (the Hunnic and Germanic migrations), economic strain, plague, and political fragmentation. The single-cause explanations have all been undermined by the evidence; the multi-causal accounts are inevitably less satisfying as narrative but better-supported.

concepts.title: Han China and the Mauryan World
concepts.contentHtml:
The contemporaneous empires of East and South Asia produced equally significant imperial traditions. The Han dynasty (206 BCE – 220 CE) consolidated the Qin unification of China into a four-century imperial order that established the institutional template for Chinese empire through the 20th century. Han contributions included the civil-service examination system (in nascent form, expanded in later dynasties), Confucian ideological orthodoxy, the long-distance Silk Road trade networks, and the bureaucratic shibing administration that allowed central control over a vast and culturally diverse population.

The Han combination of territorial scale (perhaps 60 million subjects, comparable to contemporaneous Rome) with institutional depth (a literate bureaucracy, a codified legal system, a recognised ideology) produced a model of imperial governance that survived multiple subsequent dynastic cycles. The 'Tianxia' (天下, 'all under heaven') frame organised Chinese imperial thinking around a central civilisation surrounded by tributary peripheries — a different ideological structure from the Roman conception of distinct subject provinces.

The Mauryan Empire in India (322–185 BCE) under Chandragupta and Ashoka produced one of the most remarkable single political experiments of antiquity. Ashoka's post-Kalinga conversion to Buddhist principles and his subsequent edicts (carved on rocks and pillars across the empire) articulated a doctrine of just rule, religious tolerance, and concern for subject welfare that has no clear parallel in contemporaneous imperial traditions. The empire's institutional sophistication — the arthashastra attributed to Kautilya is one of the most detailed surviving treatises on premodern statecraft — was matched by its rapid post-Ashokan decline, illustrating how dependent imperial integration could be on the personal capacity of its rulers.

title: Early Modern Colonialism
description: Spanish, Portuguese, Dutch, British — Atlantic slavery and the joint-stock empire

concepts.title: The Iberian Conquest of the Americas
concepts.contentHtml:
The European empires of the early modern period (roughly 1492–1800) were qualitatively different from earlier empires in scale, transoceanic reach, and the demographic and ecological consequences they produced. The pattern began with Spain and Portugal's post-1492 expansion, conducted under religious-political authority granted by the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas, which formally divided non-Christian lands between the two crowns.

The Spanish conquest of the Americas was unprecedented in its rapidity. Hernán Cortés's 1519–1521 conquest of the Aztec Empire and Francisco Pizarro's 1532–1533 conquest of the Inca Empire saw small Spanish forces (a few hundred soldiers each, with horses, steel weapons, and gunpowder) overthrow large indigenous polities through a combination of military advantage, alliances with indigenous enemies of the imperial centres, and — most consequentially — the spread of Old World diseases (smallpox, measles, typhus, influenza) to which American populations had no immunity. The demographic catastrophe is the central fact of early colonial history: estimates vary, but the indigenous American population probably fell by 70–90% between 1492 and 1650 across the hemisphere.

The Spanish established the encomienda system — Spanish colonists were granted rights to indigenous labour and tribute in exchange for ostensible religious instruction — and later the hacienda and plantation systems. Vast silver flows from Potosí (in modern Bolivia) and Mexican mines underwrote Spain's European wars and reshaped global trade flows; silver minted in the Americas became the dominant medium of long-distance trade across Eurasia, supporting the integration of New World, European, and Asian economies that historians including Andre Gunder Frank have called the early-modern global economy.

concepts.title: The Atlantic Slave Trade
concepts.contentHtml:
The single most consequential institutional creation of early modern colonialism was the transatlantic slave trade. Between roughly 1500 and 1870, an estimated 12.5 million Africans were forcibly transported across the Atlantic; perhaps 10.7 million survived the Middle Passage. The trade peaked in the late 18th century and was driven primarily by the labour demands of New World plantation agriculture — sugar above all, but also tobacco, coffee, indigo, rice, and cotton.

The economic mechanism was the plantation: a large agricultural enterprise producing a single export crop using enslaved labour under brutal conditions. Sugar plantations in the Caribbean (Saint-Domingue, Jamaica, Cuba, Brazil's Bahia) operated at scales that required continuous slave imports because death rates exceeded birth rates. The Caribbean plantation system was, in Sidney Mintz's analysis, one of the first industrial enterprises — labour was disciplined by the clock, production was organised in continuous shifts, and the output fed into early-modern European mass consumption (sugared tea, coffee, chocolate) at a scale that earlier economies could not have supported.

The slave trade's political-economy consequences were enormous. Profits from the trade and from plantation agriculture financed European industrialisation; the historian Eric Williams's Capitalism and Slavery (1944) argued that slavery's profits funded the British industrial revolution, a thesis that has been refined but broadly supported by subsequent scholarship. The demographic and political consequences for Africa — depopulation of source regions, the militarisation of African states involved in the trade, the long-term distortion of West and Central African political trajectories — are still the subject of active scholarly research, including by economists Nathan Nunn and others using contemporary data to identify long-run economic effects.

concepts.title: The Joint-Stock Empire and Asian Trade
concepts.contentHtml:
The 17th-century innovation that distinguished British and Dutch empires from their Iberian predecessors was the chartered joint-stock company. The Dutch East India Company (VOC, founded 1602) and the English East India Company (EIC, founded 1600) were granted monopoly trading rights, the authority to maintain armed forces, conduct diplomacy, and govern territory in Asia in the name of their home governments. The combination of corporate organisation with sovereign powers produced one of the most distinctive institutional innovations of the early modern period.

The VOC dominated the Indian Ocean spice trade through the 17th century, controlling the Indonesian archipelago and the Cape of Good Hope, with a network of fortified factories from Persia to Japan. At its peak it employed over 50,000 people and was the largest single commercial enterprise in the world. Its 1799 dissolution (after a long decline) transferred its territorial holdings to the Dutch state, producing the modern Indonesian colony.

The EIC followed a similar trajectory. From early 17th-century trading posts at Surat and Madras, the company progressively expanded its territorial control after the Battle of Plassey (1757), eventually administering most of the Indian subcontinent until the 1857 Indian Rebellion produced direct Crown rule (the Raj) in 1858. The EIC's combination of commercial monopoly, military capacity, and territorial administration prefigured the corporate-state hybrids that have re-emerged in different forms in contemporary economic governance. Its Indian operations also produced the opium trade with China that drove the 19th-century Opium Wars and the early-globalisation patterns of resource extraction whose consequences still shape Asian and African political economies.

title: High Imperialism (1870–1914)
description: Scramble for Africa, the new imperialism, Lenin's theory of imperialism

concepts.title: The New Imperialism and the Scramble for Africa
concepts.contentHtml:
The period roughly 1870–1914 saw a sharp acceleration of European territorial expansion, particularly in Africa and Asia, distinguished from earlier colonial expansion by its rapidity, the role of newer imperial powers (Germany, Italy, Belgium, Japan, the United States), and its industrial-economic motivations. Historians often label this period the 'new imperialism' to mark the discontinuity from the earlier Iberian and trading-company empires.

The Scramble for Africa is the canonical case. In 1870, European powers controlled roughly 10% of African territory, mostly coastal trading enclaves. By 1914 they controlled around 90%, with only Ethiopia and Liberia retaining nominal independence. The 1884–1885 Berlin Conference, convened by Bismarck, formalised the diplomatic rules under which European powers carved up the continent without African participation — a meeting whose maps still substantially define modern African borders.

The motivations were a complex mix. Industrial demand for raw materials (rubber, copper, palm oil, cotton) and markets for manufactured goods drove some expansion. Strategic competition — control of the Suez Canal, the Cape route, the Mediterranean — drove other expansion. Christian missionary commitments and the broader civilising mission ideology provided ideological cover. Public opinion in metropolitan countries, mobilised by sensational press coverage of figures like Stanley, Livingstone, and Gordon, made imperial expansion electorally popular. The result was that, for thirty years, European governments competed to acquire African territory at a pace and scale that earlier centuries had not seen.

concepts.title: Lenin and Theories of Imperialism
concepts.contentHtml:
The most influential single theoretical account of high imperialism was Vladimir Lenin's Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism (1917), drawing on earlier work by John A. Hobson (Imperialism: A Study, 1902), Rudolf Hilferding (Finance Capital, 1910), and Rosa Luxemburg (The Accumulation of Capital, 1913). Lenin's argument: imperialism is not a policy choice but a necessary stage of capitalism, in which accumulated capital can no longer find profitable investment opportunities at home and must be exported to colonial peripheries.

The mechanism is the monopoly phase of capitalism in advanced economies. Concentrated industrial and finance capital seeks higher returns abroad than the saturated home market can provide. Imperial state power is then deployed to secure overseas investment opportunities and protect them from local resistance and rival imperial powers. The First World War, on this analysis, was an inter-imperialist war driven by the inability of competing empires to share global investment and trading opportunities peacefully.

The thesis has been critiqued in detail. Joseph Schumpeter's Imperialism and Social Classes (1919) argued imperialism was an atavistic survival of pre-capitalist warrior elites, not a necessary phase of capitalism. Cain and Hopkins's British Imperialism (1993) emphasised the City of London's gentlemanly capitalism as the driver of British expansion, supporting parts of the Hobson-Lenin analysis. Niall Ferguson's revisionist accounts of empire have argued for net positive economic effects of British imperial rule, contested by post-colonial historians. The honest scholarly assessment is that economic motivations played a substantial role but cannot fully explain the timing, geographical pattern, or specific decisions of high imperialism — strategic, ideological, and domestic-political factors mattered too.

concepts.title: Empire's Costs and Resistance
concepts.contentHtml:
The human costs of high imperialism were enormous. King Leopold II's personal control of the Congo Free State (1885–1908) produced one of the most documented cases of colonial atrocity: rubber-tribute extraction enforced through hostage-taking, mutilation, and mass killing reduced the Congo population by an estimated several million; the British Foreign Office's 1904 Casement Report and the international scandal that followed forced Belgium to take direct control. The German conduct of the 1904–1908 Herero and Nama wars in South-West Africa is now widely recognised as the 20th century's first genocide. The British concentration camps in the South African War (1899–1902) caused tens of thousands of Boer and African civilian deaths.

Imperial violence was not exceptional but routine. Punitive expeditions, forced-labour systems, famines exacerbated by colonial extraction (the 1876–1879 Indian famine killed an estimated 5–8 million), and the more general subordination of subject populations were features of high imperial rule across European empires. Mike Davis's Late Victorian Holocausts (2001) connects the famines of the late 19th century to the global market integration that high imperialism produced.

Resistance was substantial throughout the period. The 1857 Indian Rebellion, the 1900 Boxer Rebellion in China, the Mahdi's 1880s uprising in Sudan, the Maji Maji rebellion in German East Africa (1905–1907), and many smaller uprisings produced sustained challenges to imperial rule. The eventual decolonisation movements of the post-1945 period drew on continuous traditions of anti-colonial resistance dating back to the high-imperial period — they did not begin in 1945 but built on a half-century of organisation, theory, and accumulated grievance that empires had failed to absorb.

title: Decolonization
description: India, Algeria, Vietnam, Africa — how empires unraveled after 1945

concepts.title: The Post-1945 Conjuncture
concepts.contentHtml:
The post-1945 dismantling of European colonial empires was one of the most consequential political transformations of the 20th century. Multiple factors converged. European exhaustion from the Second World War left the colonial powers militarily and financially incapable of sustaining their empires against determined resistance. American and Soviet Cold War rivalry produced both ideological pressure (anti-colonialism became part of US Cold War rhetoric) and practical opportunities (newly independent states could play superpowers off against each other). The United Nations, with the 1960 Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries, codified the international-legal recognition of self-determination.

The nationalist movements within colonies had often been organising for decades. The Indian National Congress had been founded in 1885; the African National Congress in 1912; the Vietminh in 1941. By 1945, these movements had built party organisations, intellectual frameworks, and (in some cases) experienced military forces ready to challenge imperial rule. The wartime Japanese occupation of Southeast Asia had broken the myth of European invincibility; the post-war Atlantic Charter had committed the Allies, however reluctantly, to self-determination principles.

The pace of decolonisation varied dramatically. India and Pakistan achieved independence in 1947 within two years of war's end. Indonesia (1949), the Philippines (1946), and most British, French, and Dutch Asian colonies followed in the late 1940s and 1950s. African decolonisation peaked in 1960 — the 'Year of Africa' that saw 17 newly independent states. The Portuguese empire, sustained by the Salazar regime's intransigence, lasted until 1974–1975 (Mozambique, Angola, Guinea-Bissau). The British formal empire effectively ended with Hong Kong's 1997 transfer to China; the French Algerian war (1954–1962) was particularly bloody, producing perhaps a million deaths and reshaping French domestic politics for a generation.

concepts.title: Patterns of Decolonisation
concepts.contentHtml:
Decolonisation took several broad forms. Negotiated transition — colonial powers handing over to organised nationalist parties without significant violence — was the pattern in much of British Africa, in India and Pakistan (despite Partition's massive violence), and in much of British Asia. The Macmillan 'Wind of Change' speech (Cape Town, February 1960) acknowledged the British government's acceptance that African independence was inevitable; the subsequent decolonisation of Ghana (1957), Nigeria (1960), Kenya (1963), and Tanzania (1961) followed broadly negotiated paths.

Armed liberation struggle was the pattern in Algeria, Vietnam, Indonesia, Kenya (the Mau Mau uprising), Mozambique, Angola, Guinea-Bissau, and Zimbabwe. The combination of metropolitan war-weariness, imperial economic costs, and sustained guerrilla resistance forced eventual withdrawal even when the colonial military situation was not formally lost. The French defeat at Dien Bien Phu (1954) and the subsequent Geneva Accords; the British recognition of Algerian independence (1962) after the eight-year war; the Portuguese military's 1974 Carnation Revolution that ended the Lisbon-Luanda-Maputo war — each illustrated the pattern.

Settler colonies produced the hardest cases. Where European populations had become demographically substantial — Algeria, Rhodesia, South Africa, Kenya — decolonisation was complicated by the question of what would happen to settler populations and their privileges. Algeria's million-strong pied-noir population fled in 1962; Rhodesian-then-Zimbabwean transition was prolonged through the 1965 Unilateral Declaration of Independence and the 1979 Lancaster House settlement; South African apartheid lasted until 1990–1994. The settler-colony pattern produced more violence, slower transitions, and more complicated post-independence politics than the negotiated-transition cases.

concepts.title: The Inheritance of Empire
concepts.contentHtml:
The states that emerged from decolonisation inherited boundaries, institutions, and economic structures shaped by their colonial pasts. The arbitrary borders drawn at the Berlin Conference and elsewhere — straight lines through pre-existing political units, multiple ethnic groups in single states, single ethnic groups split across multiple states — produced ongoing political-legitimacy problems for African successor states. The OAU (Organisation of African Unity, 1963) committed members to respecting inherited colonial borders to avoid endless border wars; the trade-off has been ongoing internal-stability problems within those borders.

The institutional inheritance varied substantially. British-style civil services, common-law systems, and Westminster-derived parliamentary institutions were transferred to former British colonies with mixed durability. French dirigiste economic institutions and centralised administrative traditions persisted in Francophone Africa. The Belgian Congo, decolonised in 1960 with essentially no preparation, descended into civil war and the 30-year Mobutu kleptocracy. The variation in post-independence institutional performance reflects in part the variation in colonial-era institution-building.

The economic inheritance was almost universally extractive. Colonial economies had been organised around export of primary commodities to metropolitan markets; the resulting monoculture dependencies (Ghana on cocoa, Zambia on copper, Liberia on rubber) left successor states vulnerable to commodity-price swings and slow to diversify. The combination of weak state capacity, extractive economic structure, and Cold War interventions made the post-independence trajectories of many former colonies much harder than their independence movements had hoped. The political-economy concept of the resource curse — that primary-commodity-rich economies tend to develop more slowly and politically more problematically than resource-poor peers — has its roots in the post-colonial experience.

title: Neocolonialism & Postcolonial Politics
description: Dependency, structural adjustment, the long shadow of empire

concepts.title: Neocolonialism and Dependency Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
The term neocolonialism was popularised by Kwame Nkrumah, the first president of independent Ghana, in his 1965 book Neo-Colonialism: The Last Stage of Imperialism. The argument: formal political independence was insufficient when economic structures, capital flows, and global political institutions continued to subordinate former colonies to their former colonisers. The new political map looked different; the underlying economic relationships had not.

The dependency theory tradition that emerged in Latin America in the 1960s and 1970s gave the analysis its most systematic formulation. Raúl Prebisch's work at the UN Economic Commission for Latin America had documented systematic deteriorations in the terms of trade between primary-commodity-exporting peripheries and manufactured-goods-exporting cores. André Gunder Frank's Capitalism and Underdevelopment in Latin America (1967) argued that core-periphery relations in the global economy actively produced underdevelopment in the periphery — the periphery was not 'pre-developed' but 'underdeveloped' in the sense of being structurally trapped.

Immanuel Wallerstein's world-systems theory (from The Modern World-System, 1974) placed the analysis on broader historical foundations, arguing that since the 16th century there has been a single capitalist world-system organised around core-periphery exchange, with intermediary semi-peripheral zones. The framework has been criticised for its functionalism and its treatment of all economic activity as serving core accumulation, but it remains one of the most influential single theoretical frameworks for thinking about long-run global inequality.

concepts.title: Structural Adjustment and the Washington Consensus
concepts.contentHtml:
The post-1980 period saw a sharp shift in the international-economic-policy environment that former colonies faced. The 1982 Mexican debt crisis and the broader Latin American debt crisis exposed the financial fragility of many developing economies. The International Monetary Fund and World Bank, joined by US Treasury and bilateral creditors, made emergency lending conditional on structural adjustment programmes (SAPs) that required policy reforms in recipient countries.

The standard SAP package — popularised as the 'Washington Consensus' by John Williamson in 1989 — included fiscal discipline, trade liberalisation, financial-sector liberalisation, privatisation of state enterprises, deregulation, and competitive exchange rates. The intellectual case rested on the failures of import-substituting industrialisation strategies in many developing countries during the 1960s and 1970s; the practical effect was that, through the 1980s and 1990s, the IMF and World Bank operated as the global enforcers of market-liberalising reforms across the developing world.

The results were mixed at best. East Asian economies (South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore) achieved high growth without following Washington Consensus prescriptions in detail. Latin American economies that did follow them produced less growth and more inequality than promised. Sub-Saharan African economies that adopted SAPs in the 1980s and 1990s often saw worse social outcomes (in education, health, infant mortality) than before adjustment. The Asian financial crisis of 1997–1998 and the IMF's controversial response further undermined Washington Consensus credibility. The post-2000 period has seen substantial revision of IMF practice and a partial movement away from the strictest SAP conditionality, though the core institutions and underlying ideological commitments have remained.

concepts.title: Postcolonial Theory and the Cultural Inheritance
concepts.contentHtml:
The intellectual movement of postcolonial theory, distinct from but related to economic dependency analysis, developed primarily in literature and cultural studies departments from the late 1970s. Edward Said's Orientalism (1978) was the foundational text, arguing that European scholarly representations of 'the Orient' had constructed a coherent system of cultural prejudice that served imperial domination — and that those representations continued to operate in post-colonial culture even after formal colonial rule had ended.

The key figures include Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak (Can the Subaltern Speak?, 1988), Homi Bhabha (The Location of Culture, 1994), Frantz Fanon (whose earlier The Wretched of the Earth, 1961, anticipated much of the later theoretical literature), Achille Mbembe, and Dipesh Chakrabarty. The tradition emphasised the cultural and epistemic dimensions of empire — how knowledge categories, literary canons, racial hierarchies, and gendered subordination structured imperial domination and outlived its formal end.

The contemporary politics of postcolonial reckoning has intensified in recent years. The Black Lives Matter movement, the 2020 Rhodes Must Fall and statue-removal debates, French and Belgian initiatives on cultural restitution, and continuing debates over reparations for slavery and colonial atrocities have brought the cultural-and-historical legacies of empire back into mainstream political debate in former metropoles. The question of whether and how former colonial powers should acknowledge, apologise for, and materially compensate for colonial harms is among the most politically contested questions in many advanced democracies as of the mid-2020s — and one whose answers will shape both domestic politics and international relations for years to come.

title: Empire in the 21st Century
description: American hegemony, Chinese tributary echoes, debates over informal empire

concepts.title: Is the United States an Empire?
concepts.contentHtml:
The question of whether the United States constitutes an empire — and if so, in what sense — has been argued throughout American history. The territorial expansion of the 19th century (Louisiana Purchase, Mexican-American War, Alaska, Hawaii) and the formal-colonial holdings after 1898 (Philippines, Puerto Rico, Guam) made the imperial claim straightforward. The post-1945 American position is more complicated.

The argument for an American empire of the post-1945 period emphasises several features. The global network of military bases (around 750 US bases in over 80 countries, more than any rival has ever maintained); the role of the dollar as global reserve currency and the resulting 'exorbitant privilege' Valéry Giscard d'Estaing identified; the structural power exercised through the IMF, World Bank, WTO, and other institutions in which the US holds disproportionate influence; the cultural reach of American media, technology, and consumer goods. Niall Ferguson's Colossus (2004) and Andrew Bacevich's American Empire (2002) both argued, from very different political starting points, that the US is recognisably an empire even if it does not formally describe itself as one.

The argument against emphasises the absence of formal colonial administration in most cases, the role of consent in alliance relationships, and the evident limits of US power (the failures in Vietnam, Iraq, Afghanistan; the inability to dictate outcomes in many crucial cases). Charles Maier's Among Empires (2006) defended a nuanced position: the US has empire-like features but is not a classical empire, and the differences matter for understanding how American power operates and how it can be expected to evolve.

concepts.title: China's Re-Emergence and the Tributary Question
concepts.contentHtml:
The post-1980 rise of China to become the world's second-largest economy — and the largest by some measures — has reopened debates about whether China is reconstituting historical patterns of East Asian regional order. The 'tributary system' that organised pre-modern East Asia around recognition of Chinese imperial centrality was substantially different from European empires (it featured ritual recognition rather than territorial control, and the periphery was often the more economically vibrant side of the relationship), but it constituted a recognisable form of regional hegemony.

Contemporary debates have asked whether China's Belt and Road Initiative (launched 2013), its growing investment and infrastructure presence in Africa, Latin America, and Southeast Asia, and its assertive foreign policy in the South China Sea constitute a re-emergent imperial project. The defenders of this characterisation point to: the asymmetric economic relationships that have emerged (e.g., Sri Lanka's 99-year lease of Hambantota Port to a Chinese company after debt difficulties); the integration of strategic infrastructure under Chinese ownership; and the pattern of political deference that small states near China increasingly show.

The critics of imperial-China framings argue that the actual mechanisms of Chinese influence remain mostly commercial, that the US-led order has its own strong asymmetric features, and that 'tributary' framings impose anachronistic categories on contemporary international politics. The honest assessment is that China has grown into a position where its choices substantially shape outcomes for many smaller states, and that the framework of analysis (empire, hegemony, sphere of influence, network power à la Castells) is contested and consequential — different framings produce different policy implications.

concepts.title: Informal Empire, Sphere of Influence, and Hegemony
concepts.contentHtml:
Beyond the US and China, the contemporary international system features several recognisable forms of imperial-or-imperial-like organisation. Russia's post-2014 reassertion in its 'near abroad' — the Crimea annexation, the Donbas war, the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the 2020 Belarus interventions, the Caucasus operations — substantially fits the pattern of imperial revanchism. The combination of military operations, energy-leverage politics, and information-warfare apparatus echoes Cold War active-measures patterns updated for the digital era.

The theoretical question of how to analyse these relationships has produced rich scholarship. John Mearsheimer's offensive realism predicts and often welcomes great-power-imposed regional orders; G. John Ikenberry's liberal internationalism emphasises the rule-based features of the post-1945 order that distinguish it from earlier imperial systems; Henry Farrell and Abraham Newman's 'weaponised interdependence' framework analyses how networks of trade, finance, and information create new chokepoints for state coercion. The 'sphere of influence' concept, partly retired after 1989, has returned to active use in analysing post-2014 great-power politics.

The contemporary moment may be unusually unstable. The post-1945 American-led order's foundations are eroding — challenged externally by Chinese and Russian assertiveness, eroded internally by US political polarisation and the policy choices of the post-2024 administration. What replaces it is unclear. The historical pattern is that imperial transitions are often violent, prolonged, and unpredictable; the late-decade question is whether the contemporary international system is in such a transition, and if so, how the major powers will manage it. The 21st century has not produced a stable resolution of how empire-like organisation is going to be organised in the post-Cold-War, post-American-unipolarity environment, and the unresolved nature of the question is one of the central political conditions of the current decade.
